title: Making adjectives agree
description: Give a Portuguese adjective the right gender and number, and put it in the right place.

guide.summary: A Portuguese adjective takes the gender and number of the noun it describes, wherever it stands. Learn which endings change, how they make plurals, and where the adjective goes.

sections.title: Adjectives in -o: four forms
sections.text: Most adjectives end in -o in the dictionary. They switch -o to -a for a feminine noun and add -s for a plural, exactly like the article in front of the noun.
steps: Find the noun the adjective describes.
Check its article: o or um is masculine, a or uma feminine.
Count: one or several?
Take the ending: -o, -a, -os or -as.
watch: The adjective follows the noun, not the person speaking: a man says uma casa nova too.
Nouns in -e can be either gender: o restaurante, a cidade. Check the article.

sections.title: Adjectives in -e or a consonant: one form
sections.text: An adjective ending in -e, and most ending in a consonant, has one form for masculine and feminine. Only the plural changes.
steps: Look at the dictionary form of the adjective.
If it ends in -e or in -l, -z or -r, keep it for both genders.
Add only the plural when the noun is plural.
watch: Never make grande, verde or triste into -a forms: granda does not exist.
Adjectives in -or and nationalities in -ês break this rule; see the next section.

sections.title: Adjectives in -or and nationalities in -ês add -a
sections.text: Two consonant endings do change for a feminine noun: -or and -ês. They add -a, and -ês loses its accent mark.
steps: Check whether the adjective ends in -or or -ês.
For a feminine noun, add -a.
With -ês, drop the circumflex: inglesa.
watch: Comparatives in -or do not change: melhor and maior stay the same for a woman.
The plurals are portugueses, ingleses and trabalhadores, without the accent.

sections.title: Plurals of -l and -z
sections.text: Most adjectives just add -s. Those ending in -l and -z change instead: -l becomes -is, and -z adds -es.
steps: Check the last letter of the adjective.
Ending in -l: replace the -l with -is (unstressed -il becomes -eis).
Ending in -z, -r or -s: add -es.
watch: Portuguese never ends a word in -ls or -zs.
Fácil and difícil take an accent in the plural too: fáceis, difíceis.

sections.title: Where the adjective goes
sections.text: Most adjectives, and every colour and nationality, come after the noun. A few very common ones usually go before it, and grande means something different in each place.

rows: um carro novo, uma casa amarela
um bom restaurante, uma boa ideia
um grande amigo, um amigo grande

steps: By default, put the adjective after the noun.
Put bom or boa before the noun.
For grande, before means great and after means big.

examples.pt: Eles moram em uma casa amarela.
examples.en: They live in a yellow house.

watch: The feminine of bom is boa, not bona.
A colour never goes before the noun: uma bolsa vermelha.

sections.title: Men and women together
sections.text: When an adjective describes masculine and feminine nouns together, it takes the masculine plural. One man or boy in the group is enough.

rows: O João e a Maria estão cansados.

steps: List the nouns the adjective describes.
If all are feminine, use -as.
If even one is masculine, use the masculine plural.

examples.pt: Meu pai e minha mãe são simpáticos.
examples.en: My father and my mother are nice.

examples.pt: A Ana e o Pedro são brasileiros.

watch: Do not match only the nearest noun: as meninas e o menino estão cansados.

sections.title: After ser and estar
sections.text: An adjective after ser or estar still agrees with the subject, even though the verb stands between them.
steps: Find the subject before the verb.
Read its gender and number.
Give the adjective after the verb the same ending.
watch: The verb must be plural too: as casas são, not as casas é.
English adjectives never change, so it is easy to forget the ending here.
